case_name: R. v. Jenkinson and R. v. Creekside Hideaway Motel Ltd.
text:
Date: 20060814

Dockets:  CR
05-03-00091 and CR 05-03-00092

(Portage
la Prairie Centre)

Indexed as:  R. v.
Jenkinson and R. v. Creekside Hideaway Motel Ltd.

Cited as:  2006 MBQB
185

COURT OF QUEEN'S BENCH OF
MANITOBA

Docket No. CR 05-03-00091

IN THE MATTER
OF:      The Appeal of Robert Jenkinson

B E T W E E N:

ROBERT JENKINSON,

)

Appearances
:

)

appellant,

)

ARTHUR J. STACEY and

)

DREW MITCHELL

- and -

)

for the appellants, Jenkinson

)

and Creekside Hideaway

)

Motel Ltd.

HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN,

)

)

respondent.

)

CYNTHIA DEVINE and

)

LISA CUPPLES

)

for the Crown (respondent)

Docket CR
05-03-00092

IN THE
MATTER OF:      The Appeal of Creekside Hideaway Motel Ltd.

A N D   B E T W E E N:

CREEKSIDE HIDEAWAY MOTEL LTD.,

)

)

appellant,

)

)

- and -

)

)

HER MAJESTY THE QUEEN,

)

)

JUDGMENT DELIVERED:

respondent.

)

AUGUST 14, 2006

CLEARWATER, J.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

Robert Jenkinson (“Mr. Jenkinson”) and his corporation, Creekside
Hideaway Motel Ltd. (“Creekside”) (also referred to as the “accused”), appeal
their convictions following trial in the Provincial Court of Manitoba (Criminal
Division).  They were convicted pursuant to
s. 8
of
The
Non-Smokers
Health Protection Act
, C.C.S.M. c. N92 (the “
Act
”), of
multiple breaches of
ss. 2
and
6
of the
Act
.  These regulatory
offences were created by amendments enacted by the Legislature in the fall of
2004 for the express purpose of protecting the health of Manitoba citizens by
prohibiting the smoking of tobacco in enclosed public places and in indoor
workplaces.  This was the clear intent of the Legislature, as evidenced in the
official report of the various debates (Agreed Book of Exhibits, tabs 1-11) and
as so concluded (properly in my view) by the learned Provincial Court judge
(see
R. v. Creekside Hideaway Motel Ltd.
,
[2005] M.J. No. 343,
paras. 1 to 27
).

BACKGROUND

[
2
]

The necessary background facts are clearly and concisely set out
by the learned Provincial Court judge in paras. 1 to 6 of
Creekside
,

supra
.  Mr. Jenkinson is the sole shareholder, officer, and
director of Creekside.  He and Creekside, under his direction, carry on
business as hotel keepers in the Town of Treherne.  Their premises and business
are “licensed premises” as that term is defined in the
Act
.  A
portion of these premises are open to and used by the public to engage in
properly licensed and regulated drinking and gaming activities.  The gaming
activities include the use of video lottery terminals (VLTs).

[
3
]

Both Mr. Jenkinson and Creekside were convicted of several counts
of breaching the prohibitions contained in the
Act
.  The gist of
the offences contained in the separate informations for each accused are that
they failed to ensure that no person smokes in a place where smoking is
prohibited by the
Act
.  They concurrently contravened other
provisions of the
Act
by failing to ensure that no ashtrays or
similar receptacles were in place as required by the
Act
and by
failing to post and continuously display the prescribed signage as required in
the premises with respect to the smoking prohibition established by the
Act
.
The Crown clearly established the facts which constitute the essential elements
or
actus reus
of these offences.  This is clear from the Agreed
Statement of Facts, the Agreed Book of Exhibits, the testimony at trial
(particularly the testimony of Mr. Jenkinson and Darcy Crisp, the public health
inspector who participated in the investigation and swore the original
informations), and the reasons of the learned trial judge.  Both accused
knowingly participated in the impugned activities.

ISSUES

[
4
]

At trial, and as set out in their “Amended Notice of
Constitutional Questions”, the accused launched an attack on the
Act

by advancing three alternative positions.  They submitted:

(a)
ss. 2(1)

and
2(2)
of the
Act
were invalid, void and unenforceable as being

ultra vires
to the Manitoba Legislature.  They were, in pith and
substance, criminal law which is exclusively within the jurisdiction of the
Canadian Parliament;

(b)     in the
alternative, the legislation was
ultra vires
to the Provincial
Legislature as it was, in pith and substance, a matter of national concern and
solely within the exclusive authority of the Canadian Parliament pursuant to
the jurisdiction of Parliament to regulate for the “peace, order and good
government” of Canada;

(c)      in the
alternative, the
Act
is invalid and unenforceable because it is
contrary to
s. 15
of
The
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

(the “
Charter
”).  It is a statute of general application in
Manitoba and by exempting or purporting to exempt the same or similar
activities on lands reserved for Indians within Manitoba (by
s. 9.4
of the
Act
),
the entire
Act
(or at least the prohibition sections) is rendered
illegal and unenforceable.  The accused submit that the operation of s. 9.4 of
the
Act
results in unequal treatment of them under the law on the
basis of race and (or) an analogous ground, contrary to s. 15 of the

Charter
.

[
5
]

On the appeal before me the accused proceeded on the sole issue
of whether the learned trial judge erred in failing to conclude that the
provisions of the
Act
challenged by the accused were of no force
and effect as being contrary to
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

THE LEGISLATION

[
6
]

The following sections of federal legislation are relevant to the
positions of the parties.  Firstly, the equality section of the
Charter

reads:

15.(1)  Equality before and under law and equal protection
and benefit of law
— Every individual is equal before and under the law and
has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without
discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race,
national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical
disability.

15.(2)  Affirmative action programs
— Subsection (1)
does not preclude any law, program or activity that has as its object the
amelioration of conditions of disadvantaged individuals or groups including
those that are disadvantaged because of race, national or ethnic origin,
colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.

Secondly, the following sections of
the
Indian Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-5 (the “
Indian Act
”)
read:

2.
(1)   In this
Act
,

. . .

“reserve”

(a)      means a
tract of land, the legal title to which is vested in Her Majesty, that has been
set apart by Her Majesty for the use and benefit of a band, and

(b)     except in
subsection 18(2), sections 20 to 25, 28, 36 to 38, 42, 44, 46, 48 to 51, 58 to
60 and the regulations made under any of those provisions, includes designated
lands;

18.
(1)  Subject to this
Act
, reserves are held by Her Majesty
for the use and benefit of the respective bands for which they were set apart,
and subject to this Act and to the terms of any treaty or surrender, the
Governor in Council may determine whether any purpose for which lands in a
reserve are used or are to be used is for the use and benefit of the band.

(2)      The Minister may authorize
the use of lands in a reserve for the purpose of Indian schools, the
administration of Indian affairs, Indian burial grounds, Indian health projects
or, with the consent of the council of the band, for any other purpose for the
general welfare of the band, and may take any lands in a reserve required for
those purposes, but where an individual Indian, immediately prior to the
taking, was entitled to the possession of those lands, compensation for that
use shall be paid to the Indian, in such amount as may be agreed between the
Indian and the Minister, or, failing agreement, as may be determined in such
manner as the Minister may direct.

28.
(1)  Subject to subsection (2), any deed, lease, contract,
instrument, document or agreement of any kind, whether written or oral, by
which a band or a member of a band purports to permit a person other than a
member of that band to occupy or use a reserve or to reside or otherwise
exercise any rights on a reserve is void.

(2)      The Minister may by permit
in writing authorize any person for a period not exceeding one year, or with
the consent of the council of the band for any longer period, to occupy or use
a reserve or to reside or otherwise exercise rights on a reserve.

31.
(1)
Without prejudice to section 30, where an Indian or a band alleges that persons
other than Indians are or have been

(a)      unlawfully
in occupation or possession of,

(b)     claiming
adversely the right to occupation or possession of, or

(c)      trespassing
on

a reserve or part of a reserve, the Attorney General of
Canada may exhibit an information in the Federal Court claiming, on behalf of
the Indian or band, the relief or remedy sought.

81.
(1)
The council of a band may make by-laws not inconsistent with this
Act
or with
any regulation made by the Governor in Council or the Minister, for any or all
of the following purposes, namely,

(a)      to
provide for the health of residents on the reserve and to prevent the spreading
of contagious and infectious diseases;

88.

Subject
to the terms of any treaty and any other Act of Parliament, all laws of general
application from time to time in force in any province are applicable to and in
respect of Indians in the province, except to the extent that those laws are
inconsistent with this
Act
or any order, rule, regulation or by-law made
thereunder, and except to the extent that those laws make provision for any
matter for which provision is made by or under this Act
.  [Underlining
supplied]

I pause to note that there is no evidence to suggest that there
are any orders, rules, regulations or by-laws in existence that are
inconsistent with the prohibition sections of the
Act
.

[
7
]

The following sections of the
Act
are also relevant:

Definitions

1(1)    In this
Act
,

“
employee
” includes

(a)      any
person who is employed by an employer to perform a service, including a
volunteer;

(b)     any
person who is engaged by another person to perform a service, whether under a
contract of employment or not, and

(c)      any
person who is receiving instruction or training, or serving an apprenticeship;

. .
.

“
enclosed public place
”
means any part of an enclosed place to which members of the public have access,
including, but not limited to,

(a)      any part of

(i)       an
office building,

(ii)      a
retail store or other commercial establishment, or

(iii)     the
common areas of a residential building or shopping mall;

(b)     a health care facility,

(c)      a day care centre or
nursery,

(d)      an educational institution
or facility,

(e)      a restaurant,

(f)      an elevator,

(g)      a licensed premises,

(h)      an
enclosed place, other than a private residence, in which a private function is
being held,

(i)       a
private club to which a member or invited person has access,

(j)      a bus
shelter, pedestrian tunnel or enclosed pedestrian walkway, and

(k)      any other place or class
of places prescribed by regulation;

. . .

“
indoor workplace
” means an
enclosed area of a building, structure, mine or other premises in which an
employee engages in work, including any eating area, washroom, corridor,
lounge, reception area, lobby, elevator, escalator, stairway, amenity area,
storage area, closet, laundry room and parking garage used by employees, and
any other enclosed area frequented by employees during the course of their
employment, but does not include a private residence;

“
licensed premises
” means
licensed premises as defined in
The Liquor Control Act
;

. .
.

“
proprietor
”, in relation to
a place, area or vehicle, means an owner, employer or other person in charge
who controls or directs the activities carried on in the place, area or
vehicle, and includes a person present who is in charge at any particular time;

. .
.

“
restaurant
” includes any
part of a coffee shop, cafeteria, sandwich stand, food court or other eating
establishment that is located in an enclosed public place and is open to
members of the public, whether or not it is licensed premises or a portion of
licensed premises;

“
shopping mall
” means a
complex of commercial establishments designed for the sale of goods or services
or both to members of the public;

No smoking in enclosed places

2.(1)   Except as permitted in sections 3 to 5.1, no person
shall in

(a)      an
enclosed public place;

(b)     an indoor
workplace;

(c)      a group
living facility;

(d)      a public
vehicle; or

(e)      a
vehicle used in the course of employment, while carrying two or more employees.

Proprietor to ensure no smoking

2(2)    The proprietor of a place, area or vehicle where
smoking is prohibited under this
Act
shall ensure that no person smokes in that
place, area or vehicle.

Exception for traditional Aboriginal practices

5(1)    Nothing in this
Act
prohibits

(a)      an
Aboriginal person from using tobacco; or

(b)     a
non-Aboriginal person from using tobacco with an Aboriginal person;

if the activity is carried out for a traditional Aboriginal
spiritual or cultural practice or ceremony.

Municipality may pass by-law

6(1)    Notwithstanding the provisions of this
Act
, a
municipal council may pass a by-law to limit or ban smoking in any enclosed public
place in the municipality.

By-law conflict

6(2)    Where there is a conflict between a provision of this

Act
or a regulation made thereunder and a provision of a by-law made by The
City of Winnipeg or another municipality under subsection (1) or
another Act of the Legislature, the provision of this Act or the regulation
governs; but the provision of the by-law governs where it is more severe or
restrictive, or more extensive in its application, than the provision of this
Act or the regulation.

Proprietor to post signs

6.1(1) In every place, area or vehicle in which smoking is
prohibited by this
Act
, the proprietor shall post, and keep continuously
displayed, signs indicating that smoking is prohibited, in accordance with the
regulations.

. . .

Ashtrays

6(2)    A proprietor shall ensure that no ashtray or similar
receptacle is placed or allowed to remain in any place or area in which smoking
is prohibited under this
Act
.

Offence and penalty: contravention of
subsection 2(2)

or section 5

8(2.1) An individual or a corporation that contravenes

subsection 2(2)
or section 5 is guilty of an offence and is liable on
summary conviction,

(a)      for a
first offence, to a fine of not less than $500. and not more than $3,000.;

(b)     for a
second offence, to a fine of not less than $750. and not more than $5,000.; and

(c)      for a
third or subsequent offence, to a fine of not less than $1,000. and not more
than $15,000.

. . .

Directors and officers of corporations

8.1     If a corporation commits an offence under this
Act
or
the regulations, a director or officer of the corporation who authorized,
permitted or acquiesced in the commission of the offence is also guilty of the
offence and is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not more than the
amount that could be levied against the corporation.

When Act does not apply

9.4     This
Act
does not apply to penitentiaries, federally
regulated airports, Canadian Forces bases or to any other place or premises
occupied by a federal work, undertaking or business,
or on lands reserved
for Indians
.  For the purpose of this section, "federal work,
undertaking or business" has the same meaning as in the
Canada Labour
Code
.  [Underlining supplied]

POSITIONS OF THE
PARTIES

[
8
]

The accused and the Crown point to and rely on the principles established
by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Andrews v. Law Society of British
Columbia
,
1989 CanLII 2 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143,
Egan v. Canada
,
1995 CanLII 98 (SCC)
, [1995] 2
S.C.R. 513, and
Law v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration)
,

1999 CanLII 675 (SCC)
, [1999] 1 S.C.R. 497.  The essential difference between the accused and the
Crown lies in the position of the accused on this appeal to the effect that the
learned Provincial Court judge erred in his interpretation and application of
the principles in this instance by applying an overly rigid or technical
interpretation and application of same to the facts before him.  The accused
urge what they describe as a more purposive application and interpretation of
s. 15 and the principles enunciated by the Supreme Court of Canada,
supra
,
and conclude that the
Act
, by virtue of the inclusion of the
exemption found in s. 9.4 for “lands reserved for Indians”, offends
s. 15(1)
of
the
Charter
and is, in the consequence, void or unenforceable.

[
9
]

Counsel for the accused summarizes the five main areas of
difference between the accused and the Crown on this appeal, as follows:

(i)      with
reference to
s. 88
of the
Indian Act
,
supra
, the accused
submit that the
Act
is a law of general application as that term
is used in s. 88.  The Crown submits that the
Act
is not a law of
general application because the Legislature has properly exercised its
legislative authority in exempting the specific geographic areas or locations
as set out in
s. 9.4
of the
Act
from the application of the law.
The Crown submits that these exemptions of certain geographic areas or
institutions make it clear that this law was not intended to apply everywhere;

(ii)      the
accused submit that it is not necessary, as the Crown urges to the contrary,
for them to be part of a distinct disadvantaged group in order to obtain the
relief sought.  This, says the accused, is not a prerequisite to making out a
claim under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
;

(iii)     without
admitting that the
Act
discriminates in any way against the
accused, the Crown submits that any discrimination is, at best, economic only
and does not arise from any of the enumerated or analogous grounds set out
specifically in
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
and discussed in the
authorities.  The accused submit that they have established the discriminatory
economic effect on them caused by the
Act
and that the
discrimination arises based on race and (or) the analogous ground of
aboriginality-residence;

(iv)     turning to
the third stage of the analysis established by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Law
,

supra
, the accused submit that they have suffered a violation of their
human dignity (or at least the accused Mr. Jenkinson has), whereas the Crown
denies that the accused have established (or can establish) a violation of
human dignity as that term has been defined.  The parties do not differ in
their interpretation of the law to the effect that in order to obtain relief
under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, the violation of human dignity
must be established (on the civil standard of proof);

(v)      the Crown
submits that the accused do not have the necessary standing to seek and obtain
the relief sought by them because
s. 15
of the
Charter
does
not apply to a corporation (Creekside).  In addition, the Crown submits that
the accused do not have standing to bring any inequality claim on behalf of
aboriginal people and that is the essence of their claim in this instance.  The
accused submit that they are not seeking
Charter
relief on behalf
of aboriginal people but in considering the issue of discrimination it is
relevant for this court to consider the discriminatory effect on aboriginal
people who reside in, work at, and (or) frequent public places and indoor
workplaces on reserve lands.  Further, Creekside, relying on the Supreme Court
of Canada decision in
R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R.
295, submits that the corporation cannot be convicted of breaching a law that
is invalid because it (the law) is in breach of the
Charter
.

ANALYSIS AND DECISION

[
10
]

I would frame the central issue in this appeal as being whether
the exclusion of aboriginal persons who own and operate otherwise lawful
businesses in enclosed public places, indoor workplaces, and licensed premises
on reserve lands (as those terms are defined in the
Act
) from the
prohibitions contained in the
Act
with respect to smoking in
these places [except for aboriginal persons using tobacco solely for a
traditional aboriginal spiritual or cultural practice or ceremony]
discriminates, in the context of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, against
people (essentially non-aboriginal persons) who own and operate similar
businesses off reserve lands.  The accused are not Indians and they do not
carry on business on reserve lands.  The enactment of the prohibitions against
smoking in these places, combined with the exemption provided for competitors (essentially
all of whom are aboriginal persons) on reserves, was found by the learned trial
judge to have a detrimental financial impact on the accused.  While I may not
necessarily agree with all of the positions advanced by the parties or accepted
by the learned trial judge, for purposes of establishing the context in which
this decision must be made, I can do no better than accept the following dicta
of the learned trial judge in his decision reported at
Creekside
,

supra
, at para. 32:

¶32     Governments regularly pass legislation that have a
profound financial impact on some citizens in relation to others.  Taxation
legislation, licensing legislation and resource legislation, to name a few, all
affect citizens in an uneven manner yet all do not give rise to a valid claim
of section 15 discrimination.  There must be more.

The learned trial judge was also
correct, in my opinion, when he set out the inquiries that a court must make to
determine whether an applicant (in this case the accused) has met the onus of establishing,
on a balance of probabilities, that an impugned law breaches
s. 15
of the
Charter
.
At para. 33 he particularized the applicable principles, as follows:

First, does the impugned law (a) draw a formal distinction
between the claimant and others on the basis of one or more personal
characteristics, or (b) fail to take into account the claimant's already
disadvantaged position with Canadian society resulting in substantively
differential treatment between the claimant and others on the basis of one or
more personal characteristics? If so, there is differential treatment for the
purpose of s. 15(1). Second, was the claimant subject to differential treatment
on the basis of one or more of the enumerated and analogous grounds? And third,
does the differential treatment discriminate in a substantive sense, bringing
into play the purpose of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
in remedying such ills as
prejudice, stereotyping, and historical disadvantage? The second and third
inquiries are concerned with whether the differential treatment constitutes
discrimination in the substantive sense intended by
s. 15(1)
.

[
11
]

Before entering into the analysis as required by
Law
,

Andrews
, and
Egan
,
supra
, I respectfully
disagree with and reject the submission of the Crown to the effect that the
Act

is not a law of “general application” as this latter term is used in
s. 88
of
the
Indian Act
.  This appears to be an attempt to justify the
decision of the Legislature to exempt some Manitoba citizens from the health
protections provided to other Manitoba citizens based on their race
(aboriginal) and (or) their aboriginality-residence (on a reserve).  Simply
because a government decides to exempt a specific location or race from the
operation of an otherwise valid law of general application, does not thereby
result in the law no longer being one of general application.

[
12
]

Turning to the first stage of the
Law
analysis, I
agree with the learned trial judge’s conclusion that the accused are not
“claimaints” who are in an already disadvantaged position within Canadian
society.  While I agree with the Crown’s submission to the effect that
s. 15
of
the
Charter
does not, and was never intended to, protect citizens
from all distinctions or differences which result from any particular law
(absent a discriminatory distinction based on one or more enumerated or
analogous grounds),
s. 15(1)
was nevertheless enacted for the purpose of
protecting
all
Canadian citizens, regardless of characteristics such as
race, ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, etc.  However, I respectfully
disagree with that portion of the learned trial judge’s conclusion (speaking of
Mr. Jenkinson) set out in para. 35 of
Creekside
,
supra
,
as follows:

¶35     … He is not being treated differently because of a
"personal characteristic" such as one of the enumerated or analogous
grounds. …

I take a different view.  All
citizens, whether members of a minority group or otherwise, are deemed equal
before and under the law and are entitled to the equal protection
and

equal benefit of the law without discrimination.  The more difficult issue
(whether or not there is discrimination as that term has been defined) comes
later in the required analysis.
Prima facie
, all citizens, which
includes citizens engaged in business, whether large or small, should be
entitled to conduct their otherwise lawful business under the same rules or
laws as their competitors, subject always to the right of any government to
enact a law for the purpose of ameliorating conditions of disadvantaged
individuals or groups as provided in
s. 15(2)
of the
Charter
.
This case is not like situations referred to by the Crown and the learned trial
judge (see para. 32 of
Creekside
,
supra
) which deal with
such matters as taxation legislation.  That type of legislation most often has
as its purpose, or at least one of its purposes, the amelioration of conditions
of disadvantaged individuals or groups as provided in s. 15(2) of the
Charter
.
That is not the case with the
Act
.  Here, for the valid purpose
of protecting the health of Manitoba citizens, the Legislature has enacted
legislation which does not provide the accused and others similarly situated
(off reserve) with the equal benefit of the law in an economic sense and at the
same time it denies citizens attending at or engaged in an otherwise lawful
activity on a reserve of the same health protection.

[
13
]

I respectfully disagree with the conclusion of the learned trial
judge, as stated by him in para. 36 of
Creekside
,
supra
,
where he referred to the
Act
and s. 28 of the
Indian Act
,
as follows:

¶36     … It cannot be a defence to a charge under a
provincial statute that a federal statute is discriminatory and the provincial
statute should be struck down.

I do not understand the accused to
submit that
s. 28
of the
Indian Act
(or any other section of the
Indian
Act
) is “discriminatory”.  Parliament has, presumably taking into
account the provisions of
s. 15(2)
of the
Charter
, validly
enacted s. 28 of the
Indian Act
which has, for all practical
purposes, the effect of prohibiting non-aboriginal persons from owning and
operating businesses on reserve lands, whether in an enclosed public place, an
indoor workplace, a licensed premise or otherwise.  It is the practical effect
of the inclusion of the exemption section (s. 9.4) in the
Act

which is in issue here; the accused submit that the exemption section does
result in discrimination against them, and other persons similarly situated, as
envisioned in
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.  In my opinion, the
situation here is analogous to the matter dealt with by the Supreme Court of
Canada in
Corbiere v. Canada (Minister of Indian and Northern Affairs)
,

1999 CanLII 687 (SCC)
, [1999] 2 S.C.R. 203.  Just as the Supreme Court of Canada determined in
Corbiere

that “off-reserve band member status should be recognized as an analogous ground”,
so should aboriginality-residence (in this case the location or residence of
persons engaged in lawful business) be recognized as an analogous ground.
Writing for the majority, McLachlin J. (now C.J.) and Bastarache J., after
agreeing with L’Heureux-Dubé J.’s opinion that aboriginality-residence
constitutes a ground of discrimination analogous to the enumerated grounds,
went on to conclude, at para. 10:

¶10     … If "Aboriginality-residence" is to be an
analogous ground (and we agree with L'Heureux-Dubé J. that it should), then it
must always stand as a constant marker of potential legislative discrimination,
whether the challenge is to a governmental tax credit, a voting right, or a
pension scheme.  This established, the analysis moves to the third stage:  whether
the distinction amounts, in purpose or effect, to discrimination on the facts
of the case.

[
14
]

Although I am satisfied that the Legislature did not intend to
subject the accused and similarly situated claimants to differential treatment
based on race or an analogous ground, I am equally satisfied that that is, in
substance, the effect of the
Act
as it currently stands (with the
exemption in place).  Unlike the learned trial judge, I conclude that the
accused have been subjected to differential treatment in the conduct of their
business and with respect to their right to work and earn their livelihood (and
create jobs and pay taxes for the benefit of all concerned) on the analogous
ground of aboriginality-residence, as that term has been explained in
Corbiere
,

supra
.  The difficult question remains as to whether, having regard to
the third stage of the
Law
analysis, the differential treatment
discriminates in a substantive sense thereby bringing into play
s. 15(1)
of the

Charter
.

[
15
]

Before turning to the third stage of the
Law

analysis, I will deal with the Crown’s submission to the effect that the
accused do not have standing to seek or obtain the requested relief.  The
decision in
Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
,
supra
, makes it clear
that although
s. 15
of the
Charter
may not apply to a
corporation, no one (an individual or a corporation) can be (or should be)
convicted of an offence, criminal or regulatory, for breaching a law that is
unconstitutional or invalid.  Moreover, I am attracted to and accept the
submission of counsel for the accused to the effect that the accused are not
attempting to seek relief on behalf of aboriginal people (who, in my view, are
entitled to the equal application of and benefit of laws such as this to
protect their health); rather, that is simply a fact to be considered in the
context of all of the provisions of the
Act
in determining
whether there is a breach of the accused’s
s. 15(1)

Charter

rights.

[
16
]

I turn to the third stage of the
Law
analysis.
Clearly, not all differential treatment, whether intended by a legislation or
whether, as in this case, being an unintended but nevertheless clear result of
the legislation in question, will result in a breach of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.
The difficult issue, as raised by the Crown, is whether the accused have, on a
subjective-objective standard, established, on balance, a loss of human dignity
or freedom by the inclusion of
s. 9.4
in the
Act
.  The Crown
says there is no loss of dignity to a business person simply because that
person might be rendered unable to meet his financial obligations or who would
suffer an economic loss (as is the case here).  This, says the Crown, is not
analogous to the violations of human dignity considered by the Supreme Court of
Canada.

[
17
]

Although I conclude, as did the learned trial judge, that the
accused are not “disadvantaged” persons, as that term is used in
Law
,

supra
, this term is nevertheless helpful in considering whether there
has been a real denial of equality.  Disadvantage refers to not only social,
political or cultural disadvantage; it also refers to economic disadvantage
when comparing persons who do not share the relevant personal characteristics
or analogous characteristics.

[
18
]

Acceptance of Mr. Jenkinson’s testimony to the effect that he
personally feels loss of personal dignity because of the effect of this
legislation on him and his business, including those who work for him, is, in
itself, not sufficient.  The more difficult issue is whether, on a realistic
objective basis, he has probably suffered a loss of human dignity, as that term
has been defined.  In
Law
,
supra
, at para. 53, Iacobucci
J. defined “human dignity” as follows:

¶53     … For the purpose of analysis under
s. 15(1)
of the

Charter
, however, the jurisprudence of this Court reflects a specific, albeit
non-exhaustive, definition.  As noted by Lamer C.J. in Rodriguez v. British
Columbia (Attorney General),
1993 CanLII 75 (SCC)
, [1993] 3 S.C.R. 519, at p. 554, the equality
guarantee in s. 15(1) is concerned with the realization of personal autonomy
and self-determination.  Human dignity means that an individual or group feels
self-respect and self-worth.  It is concerned with physical and psychological
integrity and empowerment.  Human dignity is harmed by unfair treatment
premised upon personal traits or circumstances which do not relate to
individual needs, capacities, or merits.  It is enhanced by laws which are
sensitive to the needs, capacities, and merits of different individuals, taking
into account the context underlying their differences.  Human dignity is harmed
when individuals and groups are marginalized, ignored, or devalued, and is
enhanced when laws recognize the full place of all individuals and groups
within Canadian society.  Human dignity within the meaning of the
equality guarantee does not relate to the status or position of an individual
in society per se, but rather concerns the manner in which a person
legitimately feels when confronted with a particular law.  Does the law treat
him or her unfairly, taking into account all of the circumstances regarding the
individuals affected and excluded by the law?

[
19
]

I respectfully disagree with the submissions of the Crown and the
conclusions of the learned trial judge to the effect that the evidence here has
not, on a reasonably subjective-objective basis, established that the accused
(or at least Mr. Jenkinson) have suffered a loss of human dignity as a result
of the proven effect, intended or otherwise, of the exemption of competing
businesses on reserve lands.  In my view, the right to engage in a lawful business,
whether small or large, and to work for the purpose of improving the economic
position of a person and his or her family and that of employees and their
families is a right which, if infringed, does reasonable affect a person’s
self-worth and dignity.  I pause to note that the legislators who proposed the
enactment of the amendments to the
Act
, which included the
exemption for businesses conducted on reserve lands, did not at the time (see
the report of the debates in evidence or in the Crown’s submissions before me)
suggest that this exemption was being enacted for the purposes described in
s.
15(2)
of the
Charter
; that is, to ameliorate the conditions of
disadvantaged individuals or groups, which would include aboriginal persons
wherever situate.  Rather, the Legislature appears to have simply taken the
position that it did not have jurisdiction to regulate smoking on reserve
lands.  No authority for this proposition appears to have been discussed and no
such authority was submitted to this court.  I concur with the learned
Provincial Court judge’s analysis of the so-called “jurisdictional” issue where
he discussed, at paras. 21-27, in
Creekside
,
supra
, the
rights of both provincial Legislatures and Parliament to regulate or legislate
in both different and the same or similar areas, but the learned Provincial
Court judge acknowledged that laws may have a “double aspect” to them, as is
the case here.  He properly pointed out numerous examples where federal and
provincial governments legislate (and have the right to legislate) in the same
subject area.  Just as federal and provincial governments both legislate in the
areas of gaming, securities, insolvency, and highway traffic, they both
legislate regarding tobacco control and smoking and there is no conflict
between the
Act
and other such legislation.  To suggest that a
provincial Legislature, which can and does regulate the establishment and
licensing of hotels, bars, casinos, restaurants, and gaming activities, both on
and off reserve lands, suddenly has no right to regulate smoking on reserve
lands is, with respect, incorrect.  When the Legislature attempted to do so by
enacting
s. 9.4
of the
Act
, it is reasonable for citizens such as
the accused, and others similarly situated in Manitoba society, to conclude
that their dignity and self-worth has been detrimentally affected because they
are not allowed to compete in the marketplace in the same manner as aboriginal
businesses.  Human dignity can be affected by discriminatory legislation in
social, political, and economic areas.

[
20
]

I am satisfied the evidence does support, on a reasonable
subjective-objective basis, the conclusion that the dignity and self-worth of
the accused, and others similarly situated in Manitoba society, has been
detrimentally effected.  I respectfully conclude that the learned trial judge
(and the Crown in its submissions) erred in not giving adequate weight to the
effect of legislation such as this which adversely affects the business
interests of the accused  and their right to compete in lawful economic
activities with their neighbours on a level playing field.  No one can deny the
detrimental health effects of smoking and exposure to second-hand smoke.
However, when a government decides to protect the health of its citizens by
prohibiting this activity (smoking) and the exposure to smoke in public places,
the vast majority of which (off reserve lands) are owned and operated by
non-aboriginal persons, but concurrently permits the continuance of the
impugned activity in neighbouring businesses, based on a distinction in race
and (or) aboriginality-residence, it is reasonable to assume a genuine loss of
dignity of those in the position of the accused.  This is not equal treatment
and is, in my opinion, the kind of unequal treatment contemplated by
s. 15(1)

of the
Charter
.

[
21
]

Although written 30 years ago and in the context of an attempt by
the executive branch of government to implement a policy that certain generally
applicable laws not be enforced based on membership in a specific group or race,
the following dicta of the late Chief Justice Freedman in
R. v. Catagas

(1978),
1977 CanLII 1636 (MB CA)
, 38 C.C.C. (2d) 296, of the Manitoba Court of Appeal, is as applicable
today to these circumstances as it was in 1977 to any attempt by a government
to override human rights.  He described the offending practice as follows (at
p. 301):

The other point is that nothing here stated is intended to
curtail or affect the matter of prosecutorial discretion. Not every infraction
of the law, as everybody knows, results in the institution of criminal
proceedings. A wise discretion may be exercised against the setting in motion
of the criminal process. A policeman, confronting a motorist who had been
driving slightly in excess of the speed limit,  may elect to give him
a warning rather than a ticket.  An Attorney-General, faced with circumstances
indicating only technical guilt of a serious offence but actual guilt of a less
serious offence, may decide to prosecute on the latter and not on the former.
And the Attorney-General may in his discretion stay proceedings on any pending
charge, a right that is given statutory recognition in s. 508 [am. 1972, c. 13,
s. 43(1)] and s. 732.1 [enacted idem, s. 62] of the
Criminal Code
.
But in
all these instances the prosecutorial discretion is exercised in relation to a
specific case. It is the particular facts of a given case that call that
discretion into play. But that is a far different thing from the granting of a
blanket dispensation in favour of a particular group or race. Today the
dispensing power may be exercised in favour of Indians. Tomorrow it may be
exercised in favour of Protestants, and the next day in favour of Jews. Our
laws cannot be so treated
. The Crown may not by Executive action dispense
with laws. The matter is as simple as that, and nearly three centuries of legal
and constitutional history stand as the foundation for that principle.
[Underlining supplied]

[
22
]

In the context of this
Act
, it is every bit a
breach of the
Charter
to create offences for certain conduct by
persons such as the accused and to concurrently exempt aboriginal persons from
prosecution for the same conduct.  All citizens of Manitoba are entitled to the
benefit of equal protection of their health interests from the government that
they fund through their taxes.  I also note that similar legislation
prohibiting smoking in public places (and the exposure of citizens to
second-hand smoke in public workplaces) has been enacted in other provinces
such as Saskatchewan, British Columbia, and Ontario (see Schedule “A”).  In no
instance have these Legislatures purported to exempt the business activities of
aboriginal persons on reserve lands from legislation validly enacted for health
purposes and clearly within provincial jurisdiction.

[
23
]

Having concluded that the accused and other citizens similarly
situated in Manitoba society have been discriminated against, contrary to
s.
15(1)
of the
Charter
, by the inclusion of the exemption section
(s. 9.4) of the
Act
, I turn to the required
s. 1

Charter

analysis.  That analysis is, in my opinion, not difficult.  There is no
evidence before me, and no submission which would suggest that the resulting
restrictions on the rights of the accused and others similarly situated, as
concluded above, are demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
In fact, the result of this legislation is directly to the contrary; the
accused are not treated equally, are discriminated against by this legislation,
and suffer a loss of their own human dignity while at the same time aboriginal
persons who attend and work in public places on reserves are effectively denied
the benefits of the reasonable health protection otherwise intended by the
Act
.
It is not the prohibition of smoking or allowing smoking in public places that
is, in itself, discriminatory or otherwise unconstitutional.  Rather, it is the
inclusion of the exemption section (s. 9.4) of the
Act
which
creates the discriminatory effect.

[
24
]

Having concluded that by including the exemption for reserve
lands the Legislature has discriminated, within the meaning of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
,
against the accused and others similarly situated in Manitoba society, I now
turn to the appropriate remedy.

[
25
]

While it would be inappropriate to retroactively “strike out” or
“read down” the exemption section of the
Act
as it relates to
reserve lands, the accused should not be convicted of charges laid in the face
of the discriminatory exemption section.  Their appeals are allowed and an
acquittal on all charges is directed.  As to whether it is appropriate to strike
out the entire
Act
or, as a minimum, all of the sections which
create regulatory offences, I am satisfied the approach adopted by Scurfield J.
in
Baril v. Obelnicki
,
[2004] M.J. No. 134, at para. 73
and
following, is the correct approach.  In fashioning a remedy in cases such as
this Scurfield J. concisely enunciated the central issue and principle at para.
74:

¶74     … The real issue is to determine whether or not by
altering the legislation the court is preserving the statutory objectives
albeit within constitutional boundaries.  In determining whether or not these
objectives can be met, I must be careful not to intrude into the legislative
sphere beyond what is necessary:  Baron v. Canada,
1993 CanLII 154 (SCC)
, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 416; Budreo
v. R. (2000),
2000 CanLII 5628 (ON CA)
, 46 O.R. (3d) 481 (Ont. C.A.). …

[
26
]

On the evidence before me, I have no hesitation in concluding
that I should strike out
s. 9.4
of the
Act
as it relates to
reserve lands and allow the balance of the
Act
to stand.  The
evidence of the statutory objectives of the provincial Legislature is clear;
the objectives of the government of the day that introduced the bill and of the
opposition members who spoke to the bill was to enact legislation to protect
the health of Manitoba citizens within limits imposed by the Constitution and the

Charter
(see the official record of the debates and proceedings
of the Legislative Assembly of Manitoba and the other exhibits contained in the
“Agreed Book of Exhibits”, tabs 1-20).  For reasons not clear from the record,
the Legislature ultimately determined [in error, in my view, and contrary to
the views of certain members who spoke to the issue of jurisdiction and the
views of Professor Schwartz of the University of Manitoba, as they are recorded
in the debates (tab 3, pp. 771-773)] that it did not have jurisdiction to
regulate smoking in public places on reserve lands.  For reasons not readily
apparent and not properly explained, the Legislature ultimately declined to pay
heed to what was (and should be) the overriding objective to be obtained, as enunciated
by Gerald Hawranik, the member of the opposition from the constituency of Lac
du Bonnet, at p. 772-3:

Aboriginal people are no different than other people.  They
get sick from cigarette smoke.  They contract cancer from cigarette smoke.
They have wives, they have husbands, they have children, they have
grandparents, and they are entitled to that protection as much as other
Manitobans.  They are Manitobans, and they deserve that protection that is
under this bill as much as anybody else in Manitoba. …

[
27
]

I am satisfied and so conclude that
s. 9.4
of the
Act

should be “struck out” and that by so doing the social objectives of the
Act

can and will be achieved within constitutional boundaries.  I am satisfied,
subject to any further submissions to the contrary that counsel may wish to
make, that the provincial government will allow a reasonable, but short, period
of time before enforcing the
Act
against proprietors of
businesses and other entities who operate on reserve lands.  These persons will
require a short time to effectively comply with the requirements of the
Act

as regards the posting of signs in accordance with the regulations and the
removal of ashtrays or similar receptacle.
